prompt: What makes a model multimodal?

choices.text: Its inputs or outputs include something other than text
choices.why: Right. That is the whole definition: which modalities go in and which come out.

choices.text: It was trained on more data than a text model
choices.why: The amount of training data says nothing about which kinds of input it accepts.

choices.text: It reasons about the world instead of predicting tokens
choices.why: It still predicts. A picture is turned into something counted before the model reads it.

choices.text: It runs several models at once
choices.why: That describes a cascade, which is one way to build a multimodal product, not what makes a model multimodal.

prompt: Match each model to its direction.

pairs.right: text and image in, text out

prompt: In the lab's inventory, the call recorded at 16000 Hz is 1,772,316 bytes. How many bytes is the telephone version, at 8000 Hz in mu-law?
hint: It is in the inventory, one line above.

prompt: Why is a wrong word in a transcript harder to catch than a crash?

choices.text: Because Whisper deliberately hides the words it was unsure about
choices.why: There is no intent involved. The model writes its best guess, and a wrong guess is still a fluent sentence.

choices.text: Because errors in speech models are rarer than crashes, so nobody looks
choices.why: The lab's first eight seconds already had one. Rarity is not the reason they are hard to see.

choices.text: It reads just as fluently with the error in it
choices.why: Right. Kau for Caio carries no mark of doubt; only the recording says it is wrong.

choices.text: Because a transcript has no text to check
choices.why: It is text. What it lacks is the truth beside it: the recording is where the truth is.

prompt: What makes a multimodal use case worth its cost, in every row of the table?

choices.text: Somebody's time spent on the work
choices.why: Right. If nobody was going to do the work, automating it saves nothing.

choices.text: The model is more accurate than a person
choices.why: None of the rows claims that. Several of them fail on exactly what a person gets right.

choices.text: The novelty of the feature for customers
choices.why: Novelty is not in the table. The test is whose work it replaces.

choices.text: Lower latency than a text model
choices.why: Multimodal calls are larger and usually slower, not faster.

prompt: A shop receives four supplier invoices a month as scanned PDFs. What does the section's test say about building a vision pipeline for them?

choices.text: Build it, because scans are exactly what vision models are for
choices.why: The direction fits, but the saving is four invoices of typing a month.

choices.text: Build it with two models so that one checks the other
choices.why: That doubles the cost of a job that saves almost nothing.

choices.text: It cannot be done, because vision models do not read scans
choices.why: They do, with errors. The question here is whether it pays.

choices.text: It saves minutes a month, too little to pay for it
choices.why: Right. The person's time is the saving, and here there is little of it.

prompt: Which failure belongs to the video → text direction in particular?

choices.text: Text drawn inside the picture comes out garbled
choices.why: That is the classic failure of text → image.

choices.text: What happens between two sampled pictures
choices.why: Right. A video is read as pictures sampled from it, and the gaps are unseen.

choices.text: A number is read aloud as the wrong word
choices.why: That belongs to text → audio.

choices.text: A misread digit that looks plausible on an invoice
choices.why: That is image → text, the invoice row.

prompt: Why does this course leave out deciding things about a person from their face or voice?

choices.text: The legal and ethical weight it carries
choices.why: Right. Biometric data is sensitive under the LGPD, and the weight is more than an intermediate course treats honestly.

choices.text: The models for it do not exist yet
choices.why: They exist. The reason is the weight of using them.

choices.text: It needs a GPU the lab does not have
choices.why: The section gives no hardware reason.

choices.text: It is the same as speaker separation, which lesson 5 already teaches
choices.why: Separating two voices in a call says who spoke when, not who a person is or what they are like.

prompt: In a cascade, what joins one model to the next?

choices.text: Text
choices.why: Right, and text is logged, read and measured at every joint.

choices.text: Audio, resampled at each stage
choices.why: Only the first stage hears audio and only the last one produces it.

choices.text: A shared embedding the three models were trained on together
choices.why: The three are separate models, replaceable one at a time, which is the point.

choices.text: Nothing; they run at the same time
choices.why: They run in a row, which is why their delays add up.

prompt: A voice assistant gave a wrong answer. In a cascade, what lets you tell whether it misheard or misunderstood?

choices.text: The confidence score the language model returns
choices.why: A confidence score cannot tell you which stage went wrong.

choices.text: Listening to the synthesised answer
choices.why: That tells you about the last stage only.

choices.text: Reading the transcript between the first two stages
choices.why: Right. A wrong transcript means it misheard; a right transcript and a wrong reply means it misunderstood.

choices.text: Nothing; both look the same from outside
choices.why: That is true of a native model, not of a cascade.

prompt: Which need points to a native audio model rather than a cascade?

choices.text: Keeping a transcript of every call for complaints
choices.why: If somebody needs the text, a cascade gives it for free.

choices.text: Replacing the transcriber next year without touching the rest
choices.why: Replacing one stage on its own is the cascade's advantage.

choices.text: Reacting to how upset the caller sounds, quickly
choices.why: Right. Tone is lost in a transcript, and one model is faster to wait for than three.

choices.text: Measuring each stage against its own truth
choices.why: Only a cascade has stages to measure separately.

prompt: Put the stages of a cascaded voice assistant in the order the caller's words pass through them.
In the first eight seconds of the call, what did Whisper base get wrong?

choices.text: The shop's name
choices.why: It wrote Marginalia correctly.

choices.text: The agent's name, Caio, which it wrote as Kau
choices.why: Right, both times it occurred.

choices.text: The language, which it reported as Portuguese instead of English
choices.why: It reported en, which is right.

choices.text: Nothing; the transcript matched the script
choices.why: Compare with the script: the agent's name differs.

prompt: Why did the transcript of the first eight seconds stop at "Order M."?

choices.text: Whisper cannot read order numbers
choices.why: Lesson 7 shows it writing them, wrongly at times. Here it simply had no more audio.

choices.text: The caller paused there to look for the number
choices.why: The truth file says her turn runs from 6.0 to 14.5 seconds without a gap.

choices.text: The program cut the audio at eight seconds
choices.why: Right. samples[: 8 * mmlab.RATE] is eight seconds and nothing more.

choices.text: Whisper's window is eight seconds long
choices.why: Whisper listens in windows of 30 seconds.

prompt: MediaPipe's detector looked at the invoice and said `book` with 0.51. What explains it?

choices.text: The invoice image has a picture of a book hidden in it
choices.why: The page is text and lines, drawn by the lab. There is no picture on it.

choices.text: It knows 80 kinds of thing and picks the closest one for anything new
choices.why: Right. An invoice is not one of its classes, so it reached for the nearest.

choices.text: The detector reads the titles printed on the page
choices.why: It does not read text at all; it compares shapes with the classes it knows.

choices.text: A score of 0.51 means it is not sure, so the answer is discarded
choices.why: look.py kept everything above 0.3, so it was printed, and nothing discards it.

prompt: Match each Marginalia job to the lessons that build it.
An invoice arrives as a PDF exported by accounting software. What should read it?

choices.text: A vision model, because a PDF is a picture of a page
choices.why: This PDF has a text layer: the characters are already in the file.

choices.text: Tesseract, because OCR is cheaper than a model
choices.why: OCR re-reads a picture of text that was already text, and adds errors.

choices.text: A library that reads the PDF's text layer
choices.why: Right. Exact, free and fast.

choices.text: A person, because only a person reads invoices correctly
choices.why: The characters are in the file; a program reads them exactly.

prompt: Which of these jobs need no model at all? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Refusing uploads larger than 25 MB
choices.why: Right. A file's size is a fact the file system gives.

choices.text: Reading an NF-e that arrives as XML
choices.why: Right. It is already structured data.

choices.text: Saying what a caller asked for in a recorded call
choices.why: The request is only in the audio; something has to listen.

choices.text: Finding recordings longer than ten minutes
choices.why: Right. ffprobe answers it, as lesson 1's inventory did.

prompt: Why is sending a customer's photograph to a third-party vision API a privacy question and not only a technical one?

choices.text: Because the API keeps every image it receives forever
choices.why: Retention depends on the provider's terms; the section's point holds whatever they say.

choices.text: Because photographs are too large to send safely
choices.why: Size is a cost question, lesson 13's, not a privacy one.

choices.text: Because the model may recognise the customer by name
choices.why: The transfer is the issue whether or not anything is recognised.

choices.text: It transfers the customer's personal data
choices.why: Right. A face or a document in the picture is the customer's data leaving the shop, and the privacy policy has to cover it.

prompt: Which of the course's three Ollama models do the lessons send a picture to?

choices.text: qwen2.5vl:3b
choices.why: Right. It reads pictures, which llama3.2:3b cannot, and the lessons that send an image use it.

choices.text: llama3.2:3b
choices.why: It reads and writes text only. The course uses it where the input is words.

choices.text: all-minilm
choices.why: It turns text into vectors for lesson 12's search; it neither reads pictures nor writes.

choices.text: None; pictures go to Whisper
choices.why: Whisper listens. It takes audio and gives text.

prompt: Why does `media/truth` exist?

choices.text: To measure a model against what the media really says
choices.why: Right. The media was made from a script, so the script is the truth.

choices.text: To hold the models' outputs from the last run
choices.why: It holds what the media really says, written before any model ran.

choices.text: To store the SHA-256 of every model
choices.why: Those are written in setup.sh, beside each model's address.

choices.text: To keep a backup copy of the media in case somebody deletes it
choices.why: make_media.py makes the media again whenever it is run; truth holds text and numbers, not copies.

prompt: According to `du`, how many gigabytes do Ollama's three models take in ~/.ollama/models?
`ollama list` answers `could not connect to ollama server`. What does it mean?

choices.text: Ollama's server is not running
choices.why: Right. Nothing is listening; `ollama serve` starts it.

choices.text: A model was never downloaded
choices.why: A missing model gets an answer from the server, naming the model. Here nothing answered.

choices.text: The API key in the environment is wrong
choices.why: Ollama takes no key, and a wrong key would still get an answer.

choices.text: A model file failed its SHA-256
choices.why: That is checked by setup.sh when it downloads, and says FAILED.

prompt: The command that checks a file against a written SHA-256 is `___ -c`.
A product team wants a phone line that tells callers their order status and also keeps a written log for complaints. Which design fits the section's three questions?

choices.text: A native audio model, because it is faster to wait for one model than three
choices.why: Speed is the second question. The first, whether anyone needs the text, is answered yes.

choices.text: A vision model reading the order page aloud to the caller
choices.why: The status is already data in the shop's database; nothing needs to look at a page.

choices.text: A cascade: the log needs text, and the status is in the words
choices.why: Right. The text is required anyway, and the meaning is in the words, not the tone.

choices.text: No model at all, because the order status is already in the database
choices.why: The status is, but the caller's question arrives as speech and the answer must be spoken.

prompt: Your vision model reads invoice totals and is right 98 times in 100. The accounting system takes them with nobody looking. What does the lesson say to add first?

choices.text: A check that the lines add up to the total
choices.why: Right. An independent check catches the misread digit the model wrote with confidence.

choices.text: A larger vision model with a better score on invoices
choices.why: A better model still makes the wrong value look right. The fix is a check.

choices.text: Nothing; 98% is better than most people typing
choices.why: The two in a hundred go straight into the books with nobody to notice.

choices.text: A second run of the same model on the same image
choices.why: The same model on the same picture tends to make the same mistake.
